# Graphing in Excel {#sec-graphing-excel}

Excel creates a chart from a range of cells. The important part happens before the chart menu opens: decide what one row represents, calculate the values the chart needs, and arrange them in the order the reader should see.

The workbook in this chapter uses sixty hypothetical canola fields. It contains a bar chart of mean yield by region, a line chart of mean yield by year and a scatter plot of field size against yield.

## Learning Objectives {.unnumbered}

::: {.objectives}
By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

1. Arrange a worksheet table for a bar, line or scatter chart.
2. Create a chart from a selected range.
3. Add a descriptive title and state the units.
4. Change an axis without making the comparison misleading.
5. Decide when a legend, data labels or direct labels are needed.
6. Copy a chart into a document or save it as an image.
:::

## Start With the Table {#sec-excel-chart-table}

A chart reads the cells you select. If those cells contain raw field records when the question concerns regional averages, summarize first. A chart cannot decide which calculation the question requires.

The **Bar chart** sheet in the workbook calculates one mean for each region. The **Line chart** sheet calculates one mean for each year. Their charts read those small summary tables. The **Scatter plot** uses the raw observations because each field is meant to appear as one point.

Open the workbook and look at the table beside each chart. Change a value in the **Data** sheet and the summary formulas and charts update. The formula column on the bar and line sheets shows how the values were calculated.

## Create a Chart {#sec-excel-chart-build}

Select the table, including its headers, and use the **Insert** tab to choose a chart type. Excel uses the first column as categories and the other columns as series. If the chart treats years or regions as a series, return to the source selection and check its shape.

For the three charts in the workbook:

- The bar chart selects region and mean yield, then uses a bar or column chart.
- The line chart selects year and mean yield, then uses a line chart with markers.
- The scatter plot selects acres and yield, then uses an XY scatter chart. A line chart is not a substitute here because field size is a measured number rather than an ordered label.

The chart remains linked to its cells. Editing the source values changes the chart; pasting new values outside the selected range may not. An Excel Table expands when rows are added and is usually a better source for a chart that will receive new data.

## Titles, Axes and Legends {#sec-excel-chart-elements}

Use **Chart Design > Add Chart Element** to add or remove titles, axis labels, legends and data labels. A useful chart title describes the comparison and includes the unit when the axes do not make it obvious: `Average field yield by region (bu/ac)`.

Bar charts normally need a zero baseline. Right-click the value axis, choose **Format Axis**, and check the minimum bound. The bars in the workbook begin at zero. The line chart uses a narrower vertical range because its values are positions connected through time rather than lengths measured from a baseline (@sec-chart-principles).

A legend is needed when colour or shape identifies several series. A one-series chart does not need a legend that says `Mean yield`; the title and axis already say that. For a few lines, direct labels can be clearer than a legend.

Data labels are useful when the exact values matter and there are only a few marks. Labelling every point in a scatter plot usually hides the pattern.

## Formatting the Chart {#sec-excel-chart-formatting}

Excel's default chart is a starting point. Remove borders, gridlines or colours that do not help the comparison. Keep light horizontal gridlines when readers need to estimate values from the axis. Avoid three-dimensional effects, shadows and patterned fills.

Colour can identify a group or highlight one result. It does not need to change for every bar. Keep the same colour meaning across charts in the same report.

To change the size or typeface of an element, click the element itself before formatting it. This avoids changing the whole chart when only the axis labels need attention.

## Moving a Chart Into a Report {#sec-excel-chart-export}

Copying a chart from Excel into Word or PowerPoint gives several paste options. **Paste as Picture** fixes its appearance and prevents later workbook edits from changing the document. A linked chart updates from the workbook but can break when the files are moved or sent to someone else.

Excel can also save a chart as an image from its right-click menu. PNG works for web pages and slides. Use enough width that the labels remain readable at the size used in the report.

Before handing it over, check the source range, category order, axis minimum, labels and units. Compare one plotted value with its source cell.
